# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 27 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 27 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_027_page_001.jpg

---

## Mandate 2 — Simplicity and Giving

**1** He said to me, "Keep simplicity and be innocent — be like little children who have no knowledge of the wickedness that destroys human life. **2** First, speak evil of no one, and do not listen with pleasure when someone speaks evil of another. If you do listen, you share in the sin of the slanderer, even if you yourself are blameless — for you are guilty simply by taking pleasure in hearing evil spoken. **3** Slander no one. Speak well of all people. Neither add to their sins nor diminish what is good in them." **4** "Moreover, do not be reluctant to give, and when you give, do not grumble about it; for you will come to know who is the good Rewarder of your generosity. **5** Give to all who are in need without judging who deserves and who does not. Give to all, for it is God's will that from his own gifts giving should come to all. Those who receive will give account to God for why and how they received; for those who receive in genuine need will not be condemned, but those who receive by hypocrisy will pay a penalty. **6** The giver is innocent; for just as he received from the Lord a commandment to give to all, so he must fulfill this service blamelessly. **7** Fulfill this simplicity, then, and you will live to God — and all who fulfill it will live to God."

---

### Council Notes

Mandate 2 joins two themes under the unifying concept of haplotēs (simplicity/single-mindedness):
1. **Freedom from slander** — the passive form of simplicity: not using speech to divide or damage
2. **Indiscriminate generosity** — the active form: giving to all without the complexity of judgment

The bold teaching on giving (v. 5) — "give without judging" — transfers moral responsibility entirely to the recipient. The giver is always innocent if they give from a pure heart. This is a striking reversal of ordinary prudential thinking about charity.

Parallel texts: Didache 1.5-6 has very similar language ("give to everyone who asks, and do not demand it back"), suggesting common tradition. James 2:1-7 (discriminating between rich and poor) may be the background problem this addresses.
